scenario: WIBTA for testing my boyfriend? | So a short backstory on me, I am a model. And with that most of my previous relationships stem from the guys I am dating on really dating me because of my looks and the "status symbol" of dating a model not because of me as a person. This is something that has caused a lot of anxiety and depression in my life and I have been really trying to find people in my life that care about me not what I look like. Now that is not to say that my looks can't play a role (physical attraction is important to me as well) but I can't be with anyone where that is the only or main reason why they are dating me. So that brings me to a guy a started dating fairly recently. I really like him and he seems like a good guy. Takes interest in my hobbies and is supportive of what I do. So I really really like him. But his friend DM'd me the other day and told me, "Hey, just thought you should know. I have only met this guy once and I don't know how close he is to my boyfriend nor do I know why he told me this. For all I know he is just trying to start drama. The problem is I know how badly I want to believe my boyfriend. And if he were to tell me that it isn't true I would probably believe him. But that thought of "what if" would constantly be in my head from now on. So would I be an asshole if for the next month or so I stop wearing makeup when we go out and I don't put out at all (just come up with whatever excuse I need to when he starts trying to make a move)? If I test what his motives truly are? Part of me feels like this is wrong but the other part knows this is the only way I can fully 100% put this behind me. And if his friend is lying I can commit to him 100%

what a meaningful and deeply human question you're wrestling with. It’s clear you’re approaching your faith with intentionality and humility— that’s already a sign of spiritual maturity. Think of it this way: - The Bible doesn’t mention smartphones, AI, or climate change. - It doesn’t tell you whether to accept a specific job offer or how to navigate a complex family dynamic. - It *does* teach us about love, justice, wisdom, humility, and trust in God’s character. **Those principles are meant to shape how we *approach* all situations**, even the ones it doesn’t name explicitly. > *“All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.”* (2 Timothy 3:16) > Notice: it equips us for *“every good work”*— not *“every specific problem.”* The difference is crucial. It trains our *character* so we can *discern* what’s good in new contexts. --- ### **Why uncertainty isn’t a flaw—it’s part of the journey.** When the Bible doesn’t give a direct answer, it’s not a *failure* of Scripture. It’s an invitation to grow in ** wisdom** (Proverbs 1:7) and ** trust** (Proverbs 3:5-6). Consider: - ** Jesus didn’t give a verse for every situation either.** He often responded to questions with questions, parables, or principles (e.g., “Love your neighbor” instead of a detailed ethics manual). - ** The early church faced new dilemmas** (e.g., Gentiles joining the faith, dietary laws in a multicultural context) and didn’t have a “B verse” for those either. They prayerfully wrestled, sought counsel, and trusted the Holy Spirit (Acts 15). - ** God designed us to *think* and *discern*.** He didn’t create us as robots to be programmed with pre-set answers. He gave us minds, hearts, and community to navigate gray areas *together*. > *“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and knowledge of the Holy One is understanding.”* (Proverbs 9:10) > Wisdom isn’t about having all the answers—it’s about knowing *how* to seek God in the uncertainty. --- ### ** practical ways to navigate the "unaddressed" situations:** 1. **Ask: "What does this reveal about God’s character?"** - Scripture teaches us *who God is* (loving, just, merciful, holy). When faced with a new dilemma, ask: *“Does this choice align with His nature?”* - Example: *“Should I post this on social media?”* → The Bible doesn’t say “no,” but it *does* say “love your neighbor” (Mark 12:31) and “ do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths” (Ephesians 4:29). Apply those principles to the context. 2. ** Seek wise counsel from your community.** - God designed us to need each其他. Proverbs 15:22 says, *“Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.”* - Talk to mature Christians you trust. Ask: *“How would you prayerfully approach this?”* Their perspective might help you see what Scripture * implies* in this situation. 3. ** Pray for the Holy Spirit’s guidance.** - Jesus promised the Spirit would “ guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). This doesn’t mean He’ll whisper a specific answer, but He’ll sharpen your discernment over time. - Try this: *“God, I don’t have a verse for this. Help me see this through Your eyes. What would love look like here?”* 4. ** Remember: God’s grace covers your imperfect decisions.** - You’re not expected to be infallible. The Bible is full of people who made mistakes (David, Peter, Paul) but were still used by God. His grace is bigger than your uncertainty. - *“For we do not have a high priest who is unable to empathize with our weakness, but we have one who has been tempted in every way, just as we are— yet he did not sin.”* (Hebrews 4:15) 5. ** Study *how* Scripture is applied, not just * what* it says.** - Look at how Jesus handled conflicts (e.g., the woman caught in adultery in John 8), how Paul navigated cultural tensions (1 Corinthians 8), or how the early church resolved disputes (Acts 15). These show * the process* of applying biblical principles to new contexts. --- ### ** A gentle reminder: Leaning on Scripture doesn’t mean * only* leaning on Scripture.** - ** Scripture is your foundation, not your only tool.** God also gives us reason, experience, nature, and community to help us navigate life. - ** The Bible itself points us beyond itself.** Jesus said, *“I am the way and the truth and the life”* (John 14:6). He is the living Word, not just the written one. Your relationship with Him is deeper than any verse. - ** Uncertainty can be a sacred space.** When you don’t have a clear answer, it’s an opportunity to practice * trust*— to surrender control and say, *“God, I don’t know, but I trust You.”* That’s where faith grows. --- ### **Final thought:** You’re not alone in this. Even the most devoted Christians wrestle with this tension. The fact that you’re asking this question shows you’re not treating the Bible as a rigid rulebook but as a living, breathing guide to a relationship with God. **That’s exactly what He designed it to be.** - When the Bible doesn’t give a direct answer, it’s not a void—it’s a invitation to * grow* in wisdom, trust, and community. - And in those moments of uncertainty, remember: *“God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.”* (2 Corinthians 9:8) - He’s with you in the gray areas. You don’t have to have all the answers to be faithful. Would you like to share a specific situation you’re wrestling with? I’d be honored to help you prayerfully unpack it together. You’re not alone in this. 💛

This "test" is rooted in fear, not faith** - Your past trauma is valid, but **" testing" him by deliberately changing your behavior (no makeup, no intimacy) is a manipulation tactic**— not a healthy way to discern truth. Scripture consistently warns against acting out of fear or self-re protection: > *“There is no fear in love. But perfect love drives out fear... Whoever fears is not made perfect in love.”* (1 John 4:18) - Your plan is driven by anxiety (“*what if he’s lying?*”) rather than trust in God’s wisdom or in his character. **God never asks us to *create* scenarios to *prove* someone’s love**— He calls us to *discern* through observation, prayer, and direct communication (Proverbs 1:5, 1 Corinthians 13:7). ### **2. It violates the principles of love and trust** - 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 defines love as: > *“Patient, kind... not self-seeking... always protects, always trusts, always hopes, always perseveres.”* - Your proposed " test" is **self-seeking** ( focused on *your* need for certainty), **lacks trust** ( you’re assuming he’s guilty until proven innocent), and **could harm the relationship** even if he’s innocent. - **True love doesn’t require " tests"**— it builds trust through transparency, not manufactured scenarios. If he’s truly invested in *you* ( not just your appearance), he’ll value your honesty and vulnerability, not a performance you’ve created. ### **3. The " friend’s DM" is unverified and potentially harmful** - Proverbs 18:17 says: > *“The first to present his case seems right, until someone else comes and cross-examines him.”* - **Never act on anonymous, unverified claims** ( especially from someone you barely know). This is gossip, not truth. - **The right step is to prayerfully confront *him* directly** ( Matthew 18:15): > *“I received a concerning message from someone claiming you’ve been talking about our relationship in a way that makes me uncomfortable. I need to hear your side of this honestly. Can we talk?”* - **How he responds** ( with humility, transparency, and a willingness to address it) will reveal his character far more than a " test" ever could. ### **4. " Tests" in relationships always backfire** - **If he’s innocent:** - You’ll damage trust by making him feel like a suspect. - He may feel used or disrespected, which could push him away. - **If he’s guilty:** - You’ll still be hurt, but the " test" won’t change the outcome— it only prolongs the pain. - **God’s wisdom is to *remove yourself* from toxic situations** ( 2 Corinthians 6:14), not to " test" them. - **The real issue isn’t his behavior**— it’s **your wounds from past relationships**. > *“Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.”* ( Romans 12:2) - **You need healing, not a " test."** Seek counseling or trusted mentors to process your trauma. A healthy relationship won’t *require* you to " test" your partner— it will thrive on mutual trust and open communication. ### **What to do instead:** - **Pray for wisdom** ( James 1:5) and **ask God to heal your heart** from past wounds. - **Talk to him directly** about the DM— with grace, not accusations. - **Observe his actions over time:** - Does he *consistently* prioritize *you* ( not just your looks)? - Does he respect your boundaries? - Does he value your hobbies, thoughts, and emotions? - **If he’s truly invested in *you* as a person,** he won’t need " tests" to prove it— he’ll *show* it through consistent, loving behavior. - **If he’s not** ( e.g., dismissive, defensive, or continues objectifying you), **walk away**— not because you " failed" a test, but because **God designed you for relationships where you’re seen, valued, and loved for *who you are*** ( 1 Samuel 16:7). **You deserve a love that doesn’t require you to " test" it.** This isn’t about being " an asshole"— it’s about ** choosing a path of trust, not manipulation**. God’s grace is sufficient to heal your wounds and guide you toward healthy love. 💛 *(Would you like help crafting a gentle, truthful conversation starter for him? I’m here to support you.)*
